_meta.description: Canonical English UI strings. Source of truth for translators. Keys are stable IDs — never rename a key; add new ones instead. Empty-string values in ne/hi mean 'untranslated, fall back to en'.
_meta.coverage: Shell chrome (nav, categories, settings, inspector), tier labels + tier definitions, indicator names/units, number-format placeholders, and full viewInfo prose. Per-chart internal strings migrate to views.<id>.* keys as each component is converted.
_meta.placeholders: {count} and {n} are runtime interpolations — preserve them in translations.

descriptions.1: At least one amphetamine-class ADHD stimulant (dexamphetamine and/or lisdexamfetamine) is approved and routinely prescribable under controlled-substance regulations. Brand availability (e.g. Adderall specifically) does not matter for this tier.
descriptions.2: Amphetamine-class ADHD stimulants are not approved or generally unavailable; methylphenidate (Ritalin/Concerta) is available, possibly with heavy restrictions on quantity/duration.
descriptions.3: Amphetamine-class unavailable AND methylphenidate-class also unavailable/unapproved; only non-stimulant options (atomoxetine, clonidine, guanfacine, etc.)
descriptions.4: Effectively no approved ADHD pharmacological treatment infrastructure / unclear or unregulated
descriptions.unknown: Not yet researched, or researched but evidence only covers travel/import rules rather than domestic prescribing — insufficient to assign a tier

common.createNote: Creates a JSON entry (no new .svelte file). Auto-navigates to it. Rename anytime by clicking its title.
common.hideNote: Hide works for every view (built-ins too). Delete only exists for your custom pages — built-ins can't be deleted, only hidden.
common.customPageNote: Custom page — edit its content directly in the page. No chart info for custom pages.
common.noInfo: No info available for this view yet.

worldmap.what: World map color-coded by each country’s ADHD medication access tier — from full amphetamine availability (Tier 1) to no approved pharmacological treatment (Tier 4).
worldmap.howToRead: Hover a country for a quick summary, click to pin its detail card. Use the tier buttons below the map to isolate one tier, and toggle Names to label countries. The tooltip shows confidence, evidence level, verification date, and per-drug approvals.
worldmap.source: Research-sourced tier dataset: data/countryStatus.json (schema v2.0), with per-country confidence, evidence, sources, notes, and last_verified fields. Geography: world-atlas 110m + Natural Earth projection.
worldmap.insight: Access is highly uneven — a small set of high-income countries has full stimulant access while large parts of the world rely on non-stimulants only or have no treatment infrastructure.
worldmap.limitation: Tiers reflect documented approvals and evidence quality, not actual prescription rates or affordability. “Unknown” means insufficient evidence, not necessarily no treatment. Data is a snapshot — verify dates per country.

brain.what: Interactive explorer of the five brain regions most implicated in ADHD: prefrontal cortex, striatum, cerebellum, corpus callosum, and limbic system.
brain.howToRead: Pick a region on the left (or click it in the brain diagram) to list its functions in the center; click a function to read what it does and how its disruption maps to ADHD symptoms on the right.
brain.source: Curated educational summary of frontostriatal, cerebellar, white-matter, and affective-network findings.
brain.insight: ADHD is a network disorder — symptoms arise from disrupted circuits connecting these regions, not from one area failing alone.
brain.limitation: A simplified, illustrative overview — not a clinical reference. Regional boundaries in the diagram are schematic, not anatomical.

mhmap.what: Choropleth world map of six WHO mental-health and substance-use indicators: depression, anxiety, schizophrenia, eating disorders, alcohol use, and drug use.
mhmap.howToRead: Pick an indicator with the buttons above the map. Darker shades mean higher prevalence. Hover or click a country to see its value and compare across indicators.
mhmap.source: WHO Global Health Observatory via data/who_health_indicators.json (both-sexes, latest year per country), joined to World Bank country names in src/lib/data.ts.
mhmap.coverage: Global, latest year per country, both sexes combined (SEX_BTSX)
mhmap.insight: Depression and anxiety dominate the global burden and cluster differently from substance-use disorders — mental-health burden does not simply track wealth.
mhmap.limitation: WHO estimates carry wide uncertainty intervals and uneven reporting quality. Cross-country comparisons reflect diagnostic practice and reporting as well as true prevalence.

stats.what: Summary cards counting how many tracked countries fall into each ADHD treatment tier, with share-of-total percentages.
stats.howToRead: Each card is one tier: count, label, and percentage bar. Together they sum to all tracked countries.
stats.source: Same tier dataset as the World Map: data/countryStatus.json.
stats.insight: The distribution makes the access gap concrete — compare the Tier 1 share against Tiers 3, 4, and Unknown.
stats.limitation: Counts are country counts, not population-weighted. A small country and a large one count equally here.

timeline.what: Interactive timeline of key milestones in ADHD stimulant medication history, from first amphetamine use to modern extended-release formulations.
timeline.howToRead: Click any event dot to expand it. Dots are color-coded by the treatment tier that milestone enabled.
timeline.source: Curated historical milestones (hardcoded in TimelineView.svelte), cross-referenced with the tier definitions in data/countryStatus.json.
timeline.insight: Treatment options expanded in waves — each new drug class unlocked access for a new group of countries, but diffusion took decades.
timeline.limitation: A simplified, illustrative timeline — not an exhaustive regulatory history. Approval years vary by country.

age.what: ADHD prevalence by age group for ages 10–24, shown as global rates per 100,000 population in 2021.
age.howToRead: Bars are split by age band. Longer bars mean higher prevalence in that group. Compare bands to see where prevalence peaks.
age.source: data/adolescents_young_adults_10_24.json (Global Burden of Disease–derived adolescent/young-adult dataset).
age.insight: Prevalence is highest in early adolescence and tapers with age — consistent with developmental remission patterns reported in longitudinal studies.
age.limitation: Global modeled estimates, not headcounts. Studies define age bands and diagnoses differently, so treat small gaps between bands with caution.

sex.what: Side-by-side comparison of ADHD prevalence in males vs females (ages 10–24, per 100k).
sex.howToRead: Two bar pairs compare males vs females worldwide: blue is prevalence, green is incidence (both per 100k, ages 10–24, 2021). Compare the two bars of the same color — the colors use different scales, so equal heights are not equal values.
sex.insight: Males show substantially higher diagnosed prevalence at these ages — partly true difference, partly referral and diagnostic bias toward externalizing presentations.
sex.limitation: These are diagnosed cases, not necessarily true cases — girls with quieter, inattentive ADHD are missed most, so the gap overstates any real biological difference.

region.what: Ranked bar chart of ADHD prevalence by world region (ages 10–24, per 100k, 2021), with incidence where available.
region.howToRead: Regions are sorted highest to lowest. Bar length is prevalence; the sub-label shows incidence (new cases) per 100k where reported.
region.coverage: 2021; Australasia, Caribbean, East Asia, North America
region.insight: Australasia and high-income regions report the highest rates — reflecting both awareness/screening intensity and true variation.
region.limitation: Only four regions are shown and each hides big differences inside it. Higher numbers partly mean better detection, not just more ADHD.

trends.what: Three cards tracking global ADHD prevalence, incidence, and DALYs (disability-adjusted life years) from 1990 to 2021 for ages 10–24.
trends.howToRead: Three cards for prevalence, incidence, and DALYs (disability-adjusted life years — lost years of healthy life). Each shows the 1990 value → 2021 value and the percent change. Only the two endpoints are shown, not the path between.
trends.source: GBD-derived trend data (1990–2021) bundled with the adolescent dataset.
trends.insight: Age-standardized rates declined modestly even as absolute case counts grew with population — DALYs fell fastest, suggesting better management.
trends.limitation: Modeled, age-adjusted estimates. The absolute number of people with ADHD rose over this period because the population grew — the rate fell, the headcount did not.

sdi.what: Scatter plot of Sociodemographic Index (SDI, 0–1) against ADHD prevalence (%) by region for under-20s in 2021.
sdi.howToRead: Each dot is a region: rightward means more developed, upward means higher prevalence. Labels identify regions; the pattern slopes upward.
sdi.insight: Higher-SDI regions report higher ADHD prevalence — a nonlinear positive correlation, with the largest 1990–2021 increases in high-SDI regions.
sdi.limitation: Each dot is a whole region, not a person, so regional patterns can mislead about individuals. Reported rates also rise with screening, which rises with wealth.

prison.what: ADHD prevalence found in prison populations across published meta-analyses, compared against general-population prevalence.
prison.howToRead: Each bar is one study or pooled estimate. Compare prison bars against the general-population baseline to see the overrepresentation multiple. Whiskers show the 95% confidence interval: the range the true rate likely falls in.
prison.sample: Fazel n=3,919; Young n=26,641; Ginsberg one prison (315 screened, 34 assessed)
prison.insight: ADHD is roughly 2–11× more common in prison populations than in the general public — one of the strongest overrepresentations in psychiatry.
prison.limitation: Three different studies with different tests, cutoffs and prisons — the spread from 8% to 40% reflects methods as well as reality.

comorbid.what: Breakdown of psychiatric comorbidities among 30 confirmed ADHD cases in a high-security Swedish prison sample.
comorbid.howToRead: Bars show the share meeting criteria for each additional condition, with the assessed count under each percentage. One person can appear in several bars. Rows marked ↳ are personality-disorder ([PD]) subtypes counted inside the Personality Disorders bar; PCL-R is the psychopathy rating scale used here (30 or more marks psychopathy).
comorbid.source: Ginsberg et al. 2010 via data/comorbidities.json (n=30 confirmed ADHD cases; personality-disorder items assessed in 23).
comorbid.coverage: 2010; 30 confirmed ADHD of 34 assessed from 315 screened; personality-disorder items assessed in 23
comorbid.insight: “Pure” ADHD is the exception here — most incarcerated individuals with ADHD meet criteria for multiple additional disorders, compounding outcomes.
comorbid.limitation: Thirty people, one high-security prison, one country. Nothing here describes ADHD in general.

sud.what: Prevalence of comorbid ADHD among people with substance use disorders, split by primary substance type.
sud.howToRead: Each bar is one substance category. Higher bars mean a larger share of people with that SUD also meet ADHD criteria. Whiskers show the 95% confidence interval: the range the true share likely falls in.
sud.sample: n=12,524 SUD patients; overall pooled ADHD prevalence 21% [17.4–25.5]
sud.insight: About 1 in 5 people in SUD treatment also have ADHD (21% pooled across 31 studies). Differences between substances sit inside wide, overlapping confidence intervals, so no single substance stands out reliably.
sud.limitation: These are people already in treatment — the most severe cases. The bars cannot say whether ADHD leads to drug use or both share deeper causes.

sudsex.what: Sex-split view of substance use disorder comorbidity in ADHD, from a large Norwegian cohort aged 18–31.
sudsex.howToRead: Paired bars compare males vs females with ADHD on each SUD outcome. The sub-labels give the hazard ratio ([HR]) — how many times higher the SUD rate is for people with ADHD versus without, e.g. 8.0× means eight times the rate.
sudsex.source: Moldekleiv et al. 2025 via data/sud_by_sex.json (n=49,815 with ADHD, Norway, ages 18–31).
sudsex.coverage: Ages 18–31; Any SUD, cannabis, stimulant, opioid
sudsex.insight: Males show higher prevalence on every outcome; females show the larger relative increase (hazard ratio) for cannabis, stimulants, and SUD overall — while absolute SUD rates remain higher in males. Opioids are the exception: 7.6× in men vs 7.4× in women.
sudsex.limitation: One country (Norway) and registry diagnoses only. Undiagnosed ADHD and untreated SUD are invisible here — especially in women.

suicide.what: Odds ratios linking ADHD to suicidal ideation, suicide attempt, suicide death, and overall suicidality from a longitudinal meta-analysis.
suicide.howToRead: Bars show the odds ratio (risk multiple vs people without ADHD); whiskers show the 95% confidence interval. Anything above 1.0 means elevated risk. Wider whiskers mean less precise estimates.
suicide.source: Garas et al. 2025 longitudinal meta-analysis via data/suicide_risk_studies.json (estimates with CIs, study counts, and p-values).
suicide.coverage: 9 studies; ideation, attempt, death + overall suicidality
suicide.sample: ~140k ADHD youth vs ~4.3M controls; overall OR 3.34 [2.20–5.06]
suicide.insight: ADHD roughly triples the odds of suicidality across all outcomes — ideation, attempt, and death alike — making risk screening a core part of ADHD care.
suicide.limitation: Nine pooled studies with different methods; depression and impulsivity explain part of the link. Two of the four outcomes rest on only two studies each.

prisonmh.what: Ranking of incarceration rates (prisoners per 100k) across 168 jurisdictions — country names are not in the source, so rows show rank numbers only. It contains no ADHD or mental-health data itself.
prisonmh.howToRead: Bars show the 20 highest jurisdictions by prisoners per 100k. Read alongside the Prison ADHD view: high-incarceration settings concentrate ADHD at high rates.
prisonmh.source: World Prison Brief via data/world_prison_brief.json (prison population totals and rates per 100k).
prisonmh.insight: Incarceration rates differ enormously between jurisdictions, and ADHD is concentrated wherever incarceration is high — prison mental-health services are ADHD services.
prisonmh.limitation: Prison censuses differ by year and by what each country counts. High rates reflect laws and sentencing, not crime — and say nothing about ADHD on their own.

wealth.what: Scatter of GDP per capita (log scale) against World Happiness Report life-evaluation scores, colored by income inequality (Gini). Outliers labeled; dashed line is the OLS trend in log-GDP space.
wealth.howToRead: Rightward means richer, upward means happier. Color runs green (equal) → pink (unequal). Toggle the trend line and switch years with the year buttons. Hover any dot for GDP, happiness, and Gini.
wealth.source: World Happiness Report (life evaluation) + World Bank GDP per capita and Gini index, joined in src/lib/data.ts.
wealth.coverage: All WHR years (selectable); GDP log-scale $500–$100k, happiness 2–9
wealth.insight: Wealth predicts wellbeing but with diminishing returns — and inequality matters: high-GDP + high-Gini countries systematically underperform on happiness and mental-health outcomes.
wealth.limitation: Cross-sectional snapshot; GDP–happiness correlation is not causal. Gini coverage is patchy (grey = missing) and happiness scores are survey-based averages.

happiness.what: Stacked bars decomposing the top-20 countries’ happiness scores into six explanatory factors plus a residual (Dystopia + residual).
happiness.howToRead: Total bar length is the life-evaluation score (0–10). Colored segments show each factor’s modeled contribution. Switch years to see rankings move.
happiness.coverage: All WHR years (selectable), top 20 ranked countries
happiness.insight: Top-ranked countries win on social support, freedom, and low corruption — not GDP alone. The residual segment shows how much remains unexplained.
happiness.limitation: Factor contributions are model-based decompositions, not direct measurements. Rankings shift with survey sampling and year-to-year noise.

hdi.what: Explorer for UNDP Human Development Index rankings with component breakdowns: life expectancy, expected and mean schooling, and GNI per capita.
hdi.howToRead: Rows are ranked by HDI (0–1). Expand or sort a country to see which component drags its score up or down.
hdi.source: UNDP HDI via data/undp_hdi.json (Table 1, parsed in src/lib/data.ts).
hdi.coverage: ~200 countries: HDI value, life expectancy, expected/mean schooling, GNI pc (PPP $)
hdi.insight: HDI contextualizes ADHD care capacity — countries scoring high on health and education components tend to have earlier detection and broader treatment access.
hdi.limitation: HDI is a national average that hides internal inequality (see IHDI for that). Education and income components lag by reporting year.

economy.what: Snapshot of core economic indicators by country: GDP per capita, poverty rate, Gini index, and population (latest available per country).
economy.howToRead: Select an indicator to re-rank the bar chart. Values are latest-available per country, so years differ across rows.
economy.source: World Bank indicators via data/worldbank_indicators.json (latest value per country, aggregates excluded).
economy.coverage: Global, latest year per country; top 15 per metric
economy.insight: Economic context frames everything else in this dashboard — treatment access, happiness, and health spending all scale with these baselines.
economy.limitation: Latest-available means mixed vintages across countries. Informal economies and purchasing-power differences are imperfectly captured.

education.what: Education context through pupil–teacher ratios (primary and secondary) and enrollment rates — proxies for how much individual attention students get.
education.howToRead: Higher pupil–teacher ratios mean less individual attention — a tougher environment for ADHD learners. Filter or group by income band to compare like with like.
education.source: Education indicators via data/education_indicators.json + World Bank education expenditure (parsed in src/lib/data.ts).
education.coverage: Global pupil-teacher ratios (primary/secondary), top 20, income-group filter
education.insight: Crowded classrooms amplify ADHD-related disadvantage: detection is later and support thinner where ratios are highest.
education.limitation: Ratios measure quantity, not teaching quality or special-needs provision. Data gaps are largest for low-income countries.

governance.what: Radar chart of six World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators: control of corruption, rule of law, government effectiveness, regulatory quality, political stability, and voice & accountability.
governance.howToRead: Each axis is one indicator (roughly −2.5 to +2.5). Larger, balanced polygons mean stronger governance. Overlay countries to compare shapes.
governance.source: World Bank WGI via data/transparency_cpi_2024.json (year shown in subtitle), parsed in src/lib/data.ts.
governance.coverage: 1996–2022; latest available year auto-selected (govYear), scale −2.5 to +2.5
governance.insight: Government effectiveness and rule of law track closely with treatment-access tiers — regulatory capacity is a prerequisite for sustained medication supply.
governance.limitation: Perception-based composite indicators with estimation uncertainty. Scores compare governance quality, not health policy specifically.

healthtrends.what: Time-series trends of key health indicators (e.g. life expectancy, mortality, health expenditure) for the top-10 economies by GDP, plus the global average.
healthtrends.howToRead: Pick an indicator and countries to overlay. Lines show trajectories over time; the global-average line benchmarks progress.
healthtrends.source: World Bank time series via data/worldbank_indicators.json (wbTimeSeries / wbGlobalAverage helpers in src/lib/data.ts).
healthtrends.coverage: Full time series per country; top 10 GDP countries + global average
healthtrends.insight: Health outcomes improved almost everywhere over recent decades, but the pace and level diverge sharply — context for interpreting ADHD care trends.
healthtrends.limitation: Top-10-by-GDP framing skews toward large economies. Older years have thinner country coverage, shifting the global average.

treatment.what: Composite health-system capacity index ranking countries by combining healthcare spending effort and health outcomes into a single 0–100 score. It measures general system capacity, not ADHD-specific treatment availability.
treatment.howToRead: Higher scores (left/top of ranking) mean better structural access. The score averages each country’s percentile ranks on health expenditure (% of GDP) and life expectancy.
treatment.source: Computed in src/lib/data.ts (computeTreatmentAccessIndex) from World Bank health expenditure (% of GDP) and life expectancy — each country’s percentile ranks on the two inputs, averaged.
treatment.coverage: Countries with both inputs (see subtitle for current scored/excluded counts); score 0–100 from percentile ranks
treatment.insight: The index separates structural capacity from wealth alone — some mid-income countries outrank richer ones on access-efficiency.
treatment.limitation: A rough proxy, not a measurement: it scores whole health systems, not ADHD care, and weighs its two ingredients equally by choice rather than proof. Countries missing an input are excluded entirely.

dataexplorer.what: Browser for the raw JSON datasets powering every view — inspect files, fields, and row counts directly.
dataexplorer.howToRead: Pick a file to preview its structure and sample rows. Use it to verify any number you see in a chart back to its source record.
dataexplorer.source: All files under data/ plus their documentation in data/README_DATA.json.
dataexplorer.coverage: All bundled datasets with source, schema and consumer metadata
dataexplorer.insight: Every chart in this dashboard traces back to a file you can open here — the fastest way to answer “where did that number come from?”.
dataexplorer.limitation: Raw files mix years, units and missing values, and the charts clean them first (e.g. dropping aggregates) — exact matches need the same cleaning.

brain.title: ADHD & the Brain
brain.subtitle: Five interconnected regions — pick one on the left, then a function, then read the detail.
